core: Utility as a measure of satisfaction; total utility vs marginal utility (the extra satisfaction from one more unit)
The law of diminishing marginal utility: each additional unit adds less extra satisfaction than the one before
The budget constraint: limited income and given prices define the set of affordable bundles
The utility-maximizing rule: allocate spending so marginal utility per dollar (MU/P) is equal across all goods, with the budget fully spent
How diminishing marginal utility underlies the downward-sloping demand curve (name-and-hand-off to the demand topic)
supporting: The reallocation logic: if MU/P is higher for one good, shifting a dollar toward it raises total utility until the ratios equalize
One author-constructed worked example (coffee and muffins) whose optimum is verified by brute force
outOfScope: The demand curve itself and its determinants/shifts (economics:foundations:demand)
The general 'decide at the margin, MB vs MC' principle (economics:foundations:marginal-thinking) — referenced, not re-taught
Opportunity cost and choice under scarcity as their own concepts (economics:foundations:choice, :opportunity-cost)
Formal indifference-curve / ordinal utility apparatus (kept light and intuitive)

claims.claim: Utility is the satisfaction or usefulness a consumer gets from goods and services; total utility is the cumulative satisfaction from a quantity consumed, and marginal utility is the additional utility from one more unit of consumption.
The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, as a person consumes more of a good, the additional (marginal) utility from each successive unit tends to decline.
A consumer's budget constraint is the set of consumption bundles affordable given a fixed income and the prices of goods; choosing a bundle means picking from what the budget allows.

Total utility is maximized where the marginal utility per dollar spent (MU divided by price, MU/P) is equal across all goods purchased and the entire budget is spent; if MU/P is higher for one good, reallocating spending toward it raises total utility.

In OpenStax's example, José has $56, T-shirts cost $14 and movies cost $7; his utility-maximizing bundle is 1 T-shirt and 6 movies (total utility 103 utils), where the marginal utility per dollar is equal for both goods: the first T-shirt's 22 utils / $14 and the sixth movie's 11 utils / $7 both equal about 1.57 utils per dollar.

Because later units of a good deliver less marginal utility, a consumer will buy additional units only at a lower price; this diminishing marginal utility is one reason the demand curve slopes downward, together with the substitution and income effects.

Worked example (author-constructed, arithmetic verified by brute force in Bash): with coffee at $3, muffins at $2, a $12 budget, coffee marginal utilities 30/24/15/9 and muffin marginal utilities 22/18/16/10/6/4, the utility-maximizing affordable bundle is 2 coffees and 3 muffins (total utility 110), which exhausts the budget and equalizes MU/P at 8 utils per dollar for the last unit of each good.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 6.1: Consumption Choices
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Defines total utility and marginal utility ('the additional utility provided by one additional unit of consumption'), the law of diminishing marginal utility, and the utility-maximizing rule that marginal utility per dollar (MU/P) is equalized across goods with the budget fully spent. José example verified from the page: income $56, T-shirt $14, movie $7; optimal bundle 1 T-shirt + 6 movies, total utility 103 utils, MU/P equal at 22/14 = 11/7 = ~1.57 utils per dollar. Also supports the reallocation logic and the diminishing-MU rationale for a downward-sloping demand relationship. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 verified from the book preface; REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 2.1: How Individuals Make Choices Based on Their Budget Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the budget constraint as the set of affordable consumption bundles given a fixed income and the prices of goods, and the marginal method of choosing (buy additional units while the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost). License verified CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 from the book preface; facts synthesized, no prose copied.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Section 6.2: How Changes in Income and Prices Affect Consumption Choices
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19 (also used by the demand topic). Supports the substitution effect (a price change shifts consumption toward the relatively cheaper good) and the income effect (a higher price reduces the buying power of income), which together with diminishing marginal utility explain the downward slope of the demand curve. Used only for the demand-link claim; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.
